# 10 Colour Palettes for Technical Diagrams That Pop

A visual gallery of ten distinct colour combinations for SVG technical diagrams. Each palette is demonstrated with a working diagram showing a real technical pipeline — from neon cyberpunk to pastel soft, and everything in between.

## Quick Summary

- **10 palettes** from neon cyberpunk to pastel soft
- Each palette demonstrated with a working diagram showing a real technical pipeline
- All diagrams render inline with no external dependencies
- Each uses a different colour theory approach: complementary, analogous, triadic, or single-accent

## 1. Neon Cyberpunk

Hot pink (#ff00ff), electric cyan (#00ffff), and vivid yellow (#ffff00) on deep purple backgrounds. Maximum contrast, maximum impact. Built for dark dashboards and futuristic AI tool interfaces.

## 2. Sunset Warm

Burnt orange (#ff6f00), amber gold (#ffab00), deep crimson (#bf360c), and royal purple (#4a148c). Warm and inviting, ideal for data pipeline visualisations and executive-facing docs.

## 3. Ocean Deep

Deep sea blue (#01579b), teal (#006064), cyan (#00bcd4), and seafoam (#4dd0e1). Professional and calming, the go-to palette for architecture diagrams and system design.

## 4. Forest and Earth

Forest green (#1b5e20), sage (#66bb6a), lime (#aed581), and earth brown (#4e342e). Natural and grounded, works beautifully for infrastructure-as-code and DevOps flows.

## 5. Monochrome + Red Accent

Clean greys (#f5f5f5 to #212121) with a single red (#d32f2f) highlight. Minimalist power — draws the eye exactly where you want it.

Hot pink (#ff4081), electric blue (#448aff), lavender (#b388ff), and cyan (#00e5ff) on near-black backgrounds. Nostalgic and vibrant, a love letter to the 1980s.

Soft lavender (#e8eaf6), mint (#e0f2f1), blush (#fce4ec), peach (#fff3e0), and lilac (#f3e5f5). Gentle and approachable, ideal for content and editorial workflows.

Aurora green (#69f0ae), sky blue (#40c4ff), magenta (#ea80fc), lime (#b2ff59), and cyan (#18ffff) on dark (#0d1117). Mesmerising, designed for knowledge graphs and memory systems.

## Choosing the Right Palette

| Context | Recommended Palette | Why |
|---------|-------------------|-----|
| Dark dashboards / monitoring | Terminal Green, Neon Cyberpunk | High contrast on dark backgrounds |
| Printed documentation | Monochrome + Accent, Pastel Soft | Print-friendly, minimal ink |
| Developer tooling / CI/CD | Terminal Green, Retro 80s | Familiar terminal aesthetic |
| Executive presentations | Gold and Royal, Sunset Warm | Authoritative, warm, premium feel |
| Architecture docs | Ocean Deep, Forest and Earth | Professional, calming, readable |
| Knowledge systems / AI | Aurora Borealis, Neon Cyberpunk | Vibrant, futuristic, attention-grabbing |
| Content workflows | Pastel Soft | Gentle, approachable, non-technical |

## Colour Theory Quick Reference

Each palette uses a different colour theory approach:

- **Complementary pairs** (opposite on colour wheel): maximum contrast and visual tension. Used in Neon Cyberpunk (pink vs cyan) and Monochrome + Accent (grey vs red)
- **Analogous ranges** (adjacent on colour wheel): harmony and flow. Used in Ocean Deep (blue-teal-cyan) and Forest (green-lime-sage)
- **Triadic schemes** (three equidistant colours): balanced vibrancy. Used in Aurora Borealis (green-blue-magenta) and Retro 80s (pink-blue-yellow)
- **Single accent**: one bright colour on a muted base. Used in Monochrome + Red and Terminal Green

## Technical Implementation

All diagrams use inline SVG embedded as base64 data URIs. Key design decisions:

- **Semantic colour classes** (e.g. `.nb`, `.nc`) keep the SVG readable and maintainable
- **No external dependencies** — each diagram is self-contained
- **Responsive** — `width: 100%` with `viewBox` scales to any container
- **Base64 encoding** — bypasses markdown renderer sanitisation of inline SVG content
- **Dark backgrounds** — cyberpunk, terminal, retro, and aurora palettes naturally suit dark-mode sites

The base64 approach was chosen because markdown renderers (specifically marked.js) strip SVG child elements after encountering `<style>` tags. Base64 data URIs in `<img>` tags bypass this entirely while maintaining crisp vector rendering at any zoom level.
